title: Northwest Orient Airlines 710
summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 710, a Lockheed L-188 Electra flying from Chicago to Miami, broke up in midair over southern Indiana on March 17, 1960, after unexpectedly encountering clear-air turbulence at 18,000 ft; the right wing and part of the left wing separated and the aircraft plunged into farmland near Cannelton at over 600 mph, killing all 63 aboard. Investigators found the breakup closely resembled the 1959 Braniff Electra crash near Buffalo, Texas, and traced the cause to 'whirl mode' wing flutter: when an Electra's outboard engine mounting structure was damaged, high speed or turbulence could destroy the wing. The FAA restricted Electra operations and ordered Lockheed to redesign the structure.
probable_cause: The investigation attributed the in-flight breakup to whirl mode wing flutter: damage to an outboard engine's mounting structure, combined with high speed or turbulence, produced a destructive flutter that failed the wing -- the same unresolved defect implicated in the earlier Braniff Electra crash.

factors.evidence: The in-flight breakup of the Electra closely resembled the September 1959 crash of Braniff International Airways Flight 542 ... Investigators were unable to determine the cause at the time

led the Federal Aviation Agency to place flight restrictions on the Electra pending identification of the cause, and to order Lockheed to reevaluate the aircraft's structural integrity and demonstrate its airworthiness

when an Electra with damage to the mounting structures of one of its outboard engines operated at high speeds or in turbulence, a destructive phenomenon called whirl mode wing flutter could occur, leading to wing failure

events.text: Flight 710 took off from Chicago Midway Airport at 2:38 p.m. with 57 passengers and a crew of 6.
At 3:13 p.m., passing the Scotland, Indiana waypoint at 18,000 ft, the crew reported to Indianapolis ARTC that the flight was proceeding normally.
Around the same time, U.S. Air Force B-57s operating nearby reported moderate to severe clear-air turbulence at high altitude, with one descending from 20,000-25,000 ft to 15,000 ft to escape it.

At about 3:20 p.m., in level flight at 400 mph, the aircraft's right wing separated from the fuselage, followed over six to ten seconds by the rest of the right wing and its engines; the outer left wing and its engine also broke away.

With its wings gone, the aircraft's momentum carried it more than 3 mi before it arced toward the ground, with an engine on the remaining left wing continuing to run at full power and accelerating the dive.
The aircraft struck farmland about 8 mi east of Cannelton, Indiana, nose-first at over 600 mph, leaving a crater about 15 ft deep and 30 ft wide.

title: 1960 New York air disaster
summary: On December 16, 1960, United Air Lines Flight 826, a Douglas DC-8 heading for Idlewild Airport, collided in midair with Trans World Airlines Flight 266, a Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellation descending toward LaGuardia Airport. The Constellation crashed on Miller Field in Staten Island and the DC-8 in Park Slope, Brooklyn, killing all 128 aboard the two aircraft and six people on the ground. The accident was the world's deadliest aviation disaster at the time and remains the deadliest accident in United Airlines history.
probable_cause: United 826 had only one operational VOR receiver after the other became inoperative, which presented difficulty for the pilots to identify the PRESTON intersection. ATC was not informed of the inoperative receiver. The aircraft was estimated to be traveling at 301 knots when it collided, several miles beyond the PRESTON clearance limit.

factors.evidence: United 826 had one of its VOR receivers inoperative, presenting difficulty for the pilots to identify the PRESTON intersection.
Air-traffic control was not informed that the aircraft had only one operational receiver.
The aircraft was estimated to be traveling at 301 knots when it collided with the TWA plane, several miles beyond the PRESTON clearance limit.
United Air Lines Flight 826, a Douglas DC-8, collided in midair with Trans World Airlines Flight 266, a Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellation.

events.text: United 826 advised ARINC radio that one of its VOR receivers was inoperative.
ATC issued a revised clearance for the flight to shorten its route to the PRESTON holding point by 12 mi.
The prevailing conditions were light rain and fog.
The aircraft was estimated to be traveling at 301 knots when it collided with the TWA plane, several miles beyond the PRESTON clearance limit.
